items.stem: Distinguish between error of omission and error of commission on the basis of meaning, effect on trial balance and example.
items.answer: (i) Meaning: error of omission: a transaction is wholly or partly left out; error of commission: a transaction is recorded wrongly (wrong amount, account or total). (ii) Effect on trial balance: error of omission: complete omission does not affect it; partial omission does; error of commission: some (wrong casting, wrong posting of amount) affect it; others do not. (iii) Example: error of omission: a credit purchase not recorded at all; error of commission: a credit sale to A debited to B.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each basis: (i) Meaning: error of omission: a transaction is wholly or partly left out; error of commission: a transaction is recorded wrongly (wrong amount, account or total). (ii) Effect on trial balance: error of omission: complete omission does not affect it; partial omission does; error of commission: some (wrong casting, wrong posting of amount) affect it; others do not. (iii) Example: error of omission: a credit purchase not recorded at all; error of commission: a credit sale to A debited to B.

items.stem: Varun started business with cash ₹4,00,000, bought goods on credit for ₹1,01,000, sold goods costing ₹45,000 for ₹63,000 in cash and withdrew ₹7,000 for personal use. Without listing every step, find the capital at the end and explain why total assets rose by more than capital.
items.answer: Capital ₹4,11,000; assets ₹5,12,000, liabilities ₹1,01,000
items.markingKey: Capital = ₹4,00,000 + profit ₹18,000 − drawings ₹7,000 = ₹4,11,000 (2). Assets = ₹4,11,000 + creditors ₹1,01,000 = ₹5,12,000; the credit purchase raised assets and liabilities equally without changing capital (1).

items.stem:
Ishita prepared the final accounts of Mehta Stores without considering outstanding salary of ₹12,000, prepaid insurance of ₹3,000 and depreciation of ₹20,000. She reported a net profit of ₹1,50,000.
(i) Find the correct net profit. (ii) Which accounting concepts did she ignore?
items.answer: (i) ₹1,50,000 − ₹12,000 + ₹3,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,21,000. (ii) Matching and accrual concepts (and prudence for depreciation): expenses of the year were not matched with revenue.
items.markingKey: 4 marks: (i) ₹1,50,000 − ₹12,000 + ₹3,000 − ₹20,000 = ₹1,21,000. (ii) Matching and accrual concepts (and prudence for depreciation): expenses of the year were not matched with revenue.

items.stem: In the books of Rao Stores: the purchases book shows goods bought from Pillai Agencies for ₹59,500 and ₹46,500; a debit note was issued to Pillai Agencies for goods returned ₹4,500; the cash book shows ₹41,000 paid to Pillai Agencies with discount received ₹200. items.answer: Credit balance ₹60,300: amount owed to Pillai Agencies

items.stem: Explain the following objectives of preparing financial statements: (i) To provide information to users (ii) To ascertain the result of operations.
items.answer: (i) To provide information to users: Stakeholders get information for their decisions. (ii) To ascertain the result of operations: Gross profit and net profit or loss for the period are found.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each: (i) Stakeholders get information for their decisions. (ii) Gross profit and net profit or loss for the period are found.

items.stem:
Manish says, "I am small. My book keeper writes every transaction in the books, so I already have accounting." His accountant friend Diya disagrees.
(i) Is Manish right? Explain with reference to the stages of accounting. (ii) List four things accounting would give him that book keeping alone does not. (iii) Who in his business should do each stage?
items.answer: (i) No. Book keeping covers only identifying and recording (and classifying); accounting also summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates the results. (ii) Profit or loss for the year; financial position (balance sheet); analysis of trends and ratios for decisions; reports for banks, tax authorities and other users. (iii) Book keeping by a junior book keeper; summarising, analysis and reporting by a qualified accountant.
items.markingKey: 6 marks: (i) No. Book keeping covers only identifying and recording (and classifying); accounting also summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates the results. (ii) Profit or loss for the year; financial position (balance sheet); analysis of trends and ratios for decisions; reports for banks, tax authorities and other users. (iii) Book keeping by a junior book keeper; summarising, analysis and reporting by a qualified accountant.

items.answer: (1) Machinery A/c Dr ₹30,400; To Wages A/c ₹30,400. (2) Varun's A/c Dr ₹12,100; To Ishita's A/c ₹12,100. (3) Suspense A/c Dr ₹12,700; To Jain Traders A/c ₹12,700. (4) Sales A/c Dr ₹29,700; To Furniture A/c ₹29,700. (5) Sales Return A/c Dr ₹26,000; Purchases Return A/c Dr ₹26,000; To Suspense A/c ₹52,000. Original difference: suspense debit balance ₹39,300.
items.markingKey: Entries, 1 mark each: (1) Machinery A/c Dr ₹30,400; To Wages A/c ₹30,400. (2) Varun's A/c Dr ₹12,100; To Ishita's A/c ₹12,100. (3) Suspense A/c Dr ₹12,700; To Jain Traders A/c ₹12,700. (4) Sales A/c Dr ₹29,700; To Furniture A/c ₹29,700. (5) Sales Return A/c Dr ₹26,000; Purchases Return A/c Dr ₹26,000; To Suspense A/c ₹52,000. Suspense account (1 mark): debits ₹12,700, credits ₹52,000; opening debit balance ₹39,300.

items.stem: The bank column of the cash book of Mehta Brothers showed a debit balance of ₹83,200 on 31 March 2026. Prepare the amended cash book and then a bank reconciliation statement: (1) Cheques of ₹29,100 issued to suppliers were not presented for payment by 31 March. (2) The bank collected a dividend of ₹8,200 on the firm's investments; the cash book has no entry for it. (3) A cheque of ₹9,100 deposited into the bank was dishonoured; this was not recorded in the cash book. (4) A cheque of ₹8,000 received and entered in the bank column of the cash book was not sent to the bank. (5) The bank paid an insurance premium of ₹10,300 under standing instructions; it was not recorded in the cash book.
items.answer: Amended cash book balance ₹72,000; balance as per pass book ₹93,100
items.markingKey: Amended cash book: ₹83,200 with (2) +₹8,200, (3) −₹9,100, (5) −₹10,300 = ₹72,000 (3 marks). BRS from amended balance: (1) +₹29,100, (4) −₹8,000 = pass book ₹93,100 (3 marks). Only items not yet in the cash book are entered in it; timing differences go to the BRS.

items.stem: From the following trial balance of Gauri (Reddy Retail, Nagpur) as on 31 March 2026, prepare the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet. Credit balances: capital ₹2,54,800, sales ₹4,92,000, purchases return ₹4,000, commission received ₹6,000, creditors ₹1,40,000. Adjustments: (a) closing stock ₹59,000; (b) wages outstanding ₹7,500; (c) insurance prepaid ₹5,700; (d) depreciation on machinery 15%; (e) provision for doubtful debts 2% on debtors; (f) commission earned but not received ₹3,500.
items.answer: Gross profit ₹2,43,000; net profit ₹1,06,480; balance sheet total ₹4,89,780
items.markingKey: Trading: net sales ₹4,82,500; debit side opening stock, net purchases ₹1,96,000, wages ₹37,500, carriage ₹6,000; closing stock ₹59,000 credited; GP ₹2,43,000 (2). P&L: salaries, rent, insurance ₹17,100, bad debts ₹500, PDD ₹3,420, depreciation ₹36,000; commission ₹9,500; NP ₹1,06,480 (2). items.stem: Distinguish between error of omission and error of commission on the basis of effect on trial balance, meaning and example.
items.answer: (i) Effect on trial balance: error of omission: complete omission does not affect it; partial omission does; error of commission: some (wrong casting, wrong posting of amount) affect it; others do not. (ii) Meaning: error of omission: a transaction is wholly or partly left out; error of commission: a transaction is recorded wrongly (wrong amount, account or total). (iii) Example: error of omission: a credit purchase not recorded at all; error of commission: a credit sale to A debited to B.

items.stem: Distinguish between cash basis of accounting and accrual basis of accounting on the basis of simplicity, recording, legal acceptance and matching.
items.answer: (i) Simplicity: cash basis of accounting: simple and easy to follow; accrual basis of accounting: comparatively complex. (ii) Recording: cash basis of accounting: only cash receipts and payments are recorded; accrual basis of accounting: all revenues and expenses of the period are recorded whether or not cash is received or paid. (iii) Legal acceptance: cash basis of accounting: not accepted under the Companies Act for companies; accrual basis of accounting: compulsory for companies under the Companies Act, 2013. (iv) Matching: cash basis of accounting: does not follow the matching concept; accrual basis of accounting: follows the matching concept.

(ii) The cashier of Singh Industries totalled the bank column on the debit side as ₹1,52,000 instead of ₹1,53,000.
items.answer: (i) Time gap: cheque deposited but not cleared: The cash book records it on deposit; the bank credits it on clearance. (ii) Error in the cash book: A casting error made by the firm.
items.markingKey: 2 marks each (1 identification + 1 reason): (i) Time gap: cheque deposited but not cleared (ii) Error in the cash book

items.stem: Aryan has cash in hand of ₹40,500. Record only what belongs in a simple cash book and find the closing balance: (1) Purchased goods on credit from Sharma Agencies ₹5,500. (2) Purchased goods for cash ₹30,000. (3) Purchased goods with a list price of ₹53,000 from Sharma Agencies on credit at 10% trade discount. (4) Paid rent ₹4,400. (5) Paid the proprietor's life insurance premium ₹7,000 from business cash. (6) Sold goods for cash ₹78,500. (7) Paid ₹5,000 in cash as donation to a relief fund.
items.answer: Closing balance ₹72,600; items (1), (3) are not entered
items.markingKey: Items (1), (3) involve no cash and go to other books. Receipts ₹78,500, payments ₹46,400; balance = ₹40,500 + ₹78,500 − ₹46,400 = ₹72,600.

items.stem: Prepare the accounting equation for the business of Ishaan, Guwahati, showing the effect of each transaction, and give the balance sheet totals at the end: (1) Started business by depositing ₹3,70,000 in a bank account in the name of the firm. (2) Purchased goods for cash ₹1,30,000. (3) Purchased goods for cash ₹31,000. (4) Sold goods costing ₹54,500 for cash ₹63,500. (5) Purchased goods for ₹92,000 plus CGST and SGST @ 6% each, paying by cheque. (6) Paid salaries ₹85,900.
items.answer: Assets ₹2,93,100 = Liabilities ₹0 + Capital ₹2,93,100; balance sheet total ₹2,93,100
items.markingKey: Changes (rupees): (1) A +3,70,000, L 0, C +3,70,000; (2) A 0, L 0, C 0; (3) A 0, L 0, C 0; (4) A +9,000, L 0, C +9,000; (5) A 0, L 0, C 0; (6) A −85,900, L 0, C −85,900. Final: Assets ₹2,93,100 = Liabilities ₹0 + Capital ₹2,93,100 (5 marks for the six effects, 1 mark for the final equation).

items.stem: From the following trial balance of Tara (Kapoor Brothers, Indore) as on 31 March 2026, prepare the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet. Debit balances: opening stock ₹80,000, purchases ₹5,65,000, sales return ₹4,000, wages ₹32,000, carriage inwards ₹6,500, salaries ₹72,000, rent ₹20,000, insurance ₹9,600, bad debts ₹1,500, debtors ₹94,000, cash ₹38,500, furniture ₹32,000, machinery ₹1,30,000, drawings ₹32,000. Credit balances: capital ₹2,59,600, sales ₹7,91,000, purchases return ₹4,500, commission received ₹1,000, creditors ₹61,000. Adjustments: (a) closing stock ₹1,35,000; (b) wages outstanding ₹5,000; (c) insurance prepaid ₹4,800; (d) depreciation on machinery 10%; (e) provision for doubtful debts 5% on debtors; (f) commission earned but not received ₹3,000.
items.answer: Gross profit ₹2,38,000; net profit ₹1,26,000; balance sheet total ₹4,19,600
items.markingKey: Trading: net sales ₹7,87,000; debit side opening stock, net purchases ₹5,60,500, wages ₹37,000, carriage ₹6,500; closing stock ₹1,35,000 credited; GP ₹2,38,000 (2). P&L: salaries, rent, insurance ₹4,800, bad debts ₹1,500, PDD ₹4,700, depreciation ₹13,000; commission ₹4,000; NP ₹1,26,000 (2). Balance sheet: capital ₹2,59,600 + NP − drawings ₹32,000 = ₹3,53,600; total ₹4,19,600 (2).

items.stem:
Arjun says, "I am small. My book keeper writes every transaction in the books, so I already have accounting." His accountant friend Shreya disagrees.
(i) Is Arjun right? Explain with reference to the stages of accounting. (ii) List four things accounting would give him that book keeping alone does not. (iii) Who in his business should do each stage?
items.answer: (i) No. Book keeping covers only identifying and recording (and classifying); accounting also summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates the results. (ii) Profit or loss for the year; financial position (balance sheet); analysis of trends and ratios for decisions; reports for banks, tax authorities and other users. (iii) Book keeping by a junior book keeper; summarising, analysis and reporting by a qualified accountant.
items.markingKey: 6 marks: (i) No. Book keeping covers only identifying and recording (and classifying); accounting also summarises, analyses, interprets and communicates the results. (ii) Profit or loss for the year; financial position (balance sheet); analysis of trends and ratios for decisions; reports for banks, tax authorities and other users. (iii) Book keeping by a junior book keeper; summarising, analysis and reporting by a qualified accountant.

items.stem: The trial balance of a firm did not agree and the difference was put to a suspense account. The following errors were later found. Pass rectifying entries and prepare the suspense account to find the original difference: (1) The sales book was undercast by ₹20,200. (2) The purchases book was overcast by ₹9,000. (3) Goods costing ₹29,300 withdrawn by the proprietor for personal use were not recorded. (4) Wages of ₹28,800 paid for installing a new machine were debited to the Wages account. (5) Rent paid ₹39,400 was not posted to the Rent account.
items.answer: (1) Suspense A/c Dr ₹20,200; To Sales A/c ₹20,200. (2) Suspense A/c Dr ₹9,000; To Purchases A/c ₹9,000. (3) Drawings A/c Dr ₹29,300; To Purchases A/c ₹29,300. (4) Machinery A/c Dr ₹28,800; To Wages A/c ₹28,800. (5) Rent A/c Dr ₹39,400; To Suspense A/c ₹39,400. Original difference: suspense debit balance ₹10,200.
items.markingKey: Entries, 1 mark each: (1) Suspense A/c Dr ₹20,200; To Sales A/c ₹20,200. (2) Suspense A/c Dr ₹9,000; To Purchases A/c ₹9,000. (3) Drawings A/c Dr ₹29,300; To Purchases A/c ₹29,300. (4) Machinery A/c Dr ₹28,800; To Wages A/c ₹28,800. (5) Rent A/c Dr ₹39,400; To Suspense A/c ₹39,400. Suspense account (1 mark): debits ₹29,200, credits ₹39,400; opening debit balance ₹10,200.

items.stem: The pass book of Verma Brothers showed a debit balance of ₹70,600 on 31 March 2026 (overdraft). Prepare a bank reconciliation statement to find the balance as per the cash book: (1) A cheque of ₹13,900 received and entered in the bank column of the cash book was not sent to the bank. (2) The debit side of the bank column of the cash book was undercast by ₹200. (3) Cheques of ₹28,300 issued to suppliers were not presented for payment by 31 March. (4) The bank collected a dividend of ₹3,500 on the firm's investments; the cash book has no entry for it. (5) A cheque of ₹4,100 deposited into the bank was dishonoured; this was not recorded in the cash book. (6) Cheques of ₹34,300 deposited into the bank were not credited (cleared) by 31 March.
items.answer: Balance as per cash book ₹50,300 (overdraft)
items.markingKey: Start with overdraft as per pass book ₹70,600; add (2) ₹200, (3) ₹28,300, (4) ₹3,500; less (1) ₹13,900, (5) ₹4,100, (6) ₹34,300; overdraft as per cash book ₹50,300. (1 mark per item; correct format and final balance required.)
